h1: Brewing a Belgian tripel at home without hot alcohol flavours
title: Belgian Tripel Without Hot Alcohol | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew a Belgian tripel at home without hot alcohol: grist and sugar, pitch rate, a free-rise fermentation and high carbonation.
teaser: A tripel should taste dry and spicy, not like a shot of spirit. Fermentation temperature decides which you get.
standfirst: A Belgian tripel is strong, pale and dry, often 8 to 9% ABV. Hot alcohol flavours come from a stressed, warm fermentation. Start cool, let it rise and the strength hides.
sections:
Typical tripel numbers are original gravity 1.075 to 1.085, final gravity 1.008 to 1.014, about 7.5 to 9.5% ABV and 20 to 40 IBU. Colour is deep gold. The flavour is spicy and fruity from the yeast, with a dry finish and high carbonation.

The defining feature is that it does not taste as strong as it is. A tripel that burns on the way down has a fermentation problem.

The style comes from Belgium's Trappist and abbey breweries, where a strong golden ale took the name tripel. It is one of the hardest beers to make well at home. It is also one of the most rewarding, because the ingredients are simple: pale malt, sugar, a few hops and a characterful yeast. Every flaw comes from process.
Hot alcohol is a fermentation fault

Hot or solvent-like alcohol comes from fusel alcohols, higher alcohols produced by stressed yeast. The main causes are a warm start to fermentation, too few yeast cells and too little oxygen. Fusels form early, during yeast growth, so a warm first two days is the biggest culprit. Once formed, they do not fade much with ageing.

A useful mental check: if you can smell solvent or nail varnish on the airlock during the first two days, fusels are forming. The fix for the next batch is a cooler start, a bigger pitch and more oxygen, not longer ageing. A tripel can taste warm from alcohol without tasting hot. Warmth is a gentle glow; hotness is a sharp burn on the tongue and in the nose.

For 20 litres at about 1.080:

  • 5.3 kg pilsner malt (82%)
  • 1.1 kg plain white sugar or dextrose (17%)
  • 0.07 kg aromatic malt (1%)
  • Mash at 64 to 65 °C for 75 minutes

The sugar is what makes a tripel dry. Brewing yeast ferments it completely, so it adds alcohol without body. Plain cane sugar works fine; there is no need for imported candi sugar in a pale tripel. Add the sugar in the last 10 minutes of the boil.

For about 30 IBU, use roughly 50 g of a 5% alpha hop such as Styrian Goldings at 60 minutes, plus 15 g at 15 minutes.
Pitch more yeast than you think

A tripel needs a big, healthy pitch. For 20 litres at this gravity, a large starter of a Belgian ale strain or two packs of a Belgian dry yeast is a reasonable target. Oxygenate well: pure oxygen through a stone for one minute, or vigorous shaking for several minutes. Add yeast nutrient in the last 10 minutes of the boil. Our guide to brewing a 10% beer without stalling covers yeast health at high gravity.
Start cool, then let it rise

This is the heart of a good tripel. Pitch at 18 to 19 °C and hold it there for the first two to three days. That keeps fusel production low while the yeast grows. Then let the temperature climb, a degree or so a day, to 24 to 26 °C. The warmth helps the yeast finish dry and brings out its spicy, fruity character.

Our guide to free-rise fermentation explains the idea in more depth. In Indian summers the risk is the opposite of most places: the room is already 30 °C or more. A fridge or water bath is needed to hold the start cool before you let it go.

Tripels are carbonated high, around 3 to 3.5 volumes. Standard thin beer bottles can fail at that pressure, especially in a hot room. Use heavy Belgian-style bottles or a keg. If bottle conditioning, add fresh yeast at bottling, since the original yeast is tired after 8% or more alcohol. Our guide to Belgian witbier covers the same bottle concerns at lower strength.

A tripel tastes better after a few weeks of conditioning. Carbonation builds, the yeast character settles and any rough edges soften. Taste one bottle at two weeks, one at four and one at eight. Store them cool and upright. In a warm Indian room, a tripel matures quickly but also stales sooner, so cool storage keeps it at its best for longer. Recognising the difference between fusels and normal alcohol warmth takes practice.
Time how fast you can cool the fermenter

Before brew day, test how fast your fridge or water bath can pull a fermenter back down if it climbs too fast. Fill it with warm water at 26 °C and time how long it takes to reach 19 °C. If the answer is more than half a day, add more cooling first.
faqs: What causes hot alcohol in a tripel?
Fusel alcohols from stressed yeast, usually caused by a warm start, underpitching or low oxygen.
Why does a tripel use sugar?
Sugar ferments completely, adding alcohol without body. That gives the dry finish the style needs.
How high should a tripel be carbonated?
Around 3 to 3.5 volumes, so use heavy bottles or a keg.
What temperature should I ferment a tripel at?
Start at 18 to 19 °C for two to three days, then let it rise to about 24 to 26 °C.
